title: Copper’s Contradiction Between AI and Supply
summary: LPL Research discusses copper’s pullback as AI worries weigh on prices, while tight Chinese supply and long-term infrastructure demand support copper’s outlook.

# Copper’s Contradiction Between AI and Supply


[Adam Turnquist](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/adam-turnquist.html) | Chief Cross-Asset Strategist


Last Updated: November 24, 2026


Additional Content Provided by Brian Booe, Analyst, Research


Copper has stood apart this year in the broader metals complex as its fellow record-setting metals of gold, silver, and platinum rolled over. However, as market participants have worked their way through this month’s equity market correction, what appeared to be another strong year for the red metal was quickly jeopardized.


Copper prices surged alongside artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks as investors bet on massive data center and AI infrastructure demand given its uses in power delivery, thermal management, and chip-level wiring across data centers and the electrical grid. But as funding and capital expenditures (capex) scrutiny intensified in October, this increasingly popular expression for the AI trade began falling alongside the Nasdaq-100 and AI-tilted markets. U.S. midterm elections and NVIDIA’s (NVDA) CEO uncertainty this month further stoked fears of a slowing AI buildout, leading investors to accelerate their scaling back of bullish positions while commodity traders broadly appeared to price in a slightly shallower global economic growth forecast. Through Friday’s close, copper traded on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CMX) was down 19.1% from its September high, and 1.9% lower on the year (prior to Monday’s relief rally).


### Copper Broke Below Key Support, But Remains Above its ‘AI Bull Market’ Trendline


*Source: LPL Research, Bloomberg 11/23/26 Disclosure: All Indexes are unmanaged and cannot be invested indirectly. Past performance does not guarantee future results.*


Although the go-to excuse for copper retracting year-to-date gains can be traced back to AI angst in the U.S., several global drivers also collided to pressure prices back to their March 2026 lows. A stronger U.S. dollar weighed on raw materials broadly, while speculation increased that the U.S. would refrain from refined copper tariffs — signaled by London-traded copper trading at a premium to U.S. prices — to further weigh on prices. And over the last week, bearish comments from renowned commodities investor and previous copper cheerleader Stan Druckenmiller paired with weaker Chinese economic growth, consumption, and industrial production data also dented sentiment en route to a sixth-straight weekly loss.


## A Case Study in Contradiction


The recent sell-off is particularly interesting considering it arrived when market conditions continued to tighten, which is typically a potent bullish indicator. China, the world’s largest copper consumer, offers the clearest evidence of this. Chinese supplies have diminished as large volumes of London-traded copper have been redirected from China to the U.S. over the last two years aimed to front-run potential refined copper tariffs. Add in a tight scrap market and Chinese smelters cutting production, and the result is Chinese inventories nearing their lowest levels since 2023. Further signaling short supply in financial markets are a record Yangshan premium (China’s price premium over London) and backwardation in China’s futures curve (where front-month futures trade higher than longer-dated contracts).


### Record Yangshan Premium and Backwardation Point to Tight Supply in China


## Looking Ahead


Copper trading last week was a case study in contradiction. Prices slid on mounting worries around the AI buildout and China’s sluggish economy while physical markets faced historic tightness. The metal rebounded to start the week after NVIDIA’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, but if another wave of AI jitters washes over Wall Street, copper holding above its AI bull market trendline may be a behind-the-curtain key to AI sentiment.


Meanwhile, the Chinese demand narrative may continue to dominate price action in addition to AI, but stretched bearish sentiment provides a contrarian signal and leaves markets exposed to squeezes. The supply crunch in China forces the world’s second-largest economy to increase its imports, which should help provide a floor for copper prices. Elsewhere, severe El Niño-related flooding has already disrupted production at mines in Chile (a major global producer of the red metal), and flood risk could worsen in the coming months and potentially affect Peruvian mines. On the other side of the globe, El Niño-related droughts in Southeast Asia could also constrain production given the large amount of water needed for mining. These weather-related effects are likely to support copper prices, as well as the broader commodities complex.


## The Bottom Line


Bottom line, despite recent market volatility, the longer-term outlook for AI infrastructure demand remains in place. Hyperscaler spending is still expected to grow in 2027, and regulatory hurdles to data center progress are unlikely to materially affect the buildout until at least 2028. Tight physical markets in China and the potential additional supply effects from the super El Niño are also supportive. More broadly, we continue to believe that rising resource nationalism is a tailwind for the broader commodities complex, as metals and minerals are increasingly framed as a strategic, economic, and in the interest of national security rather than simply a commodity trade. Constraints on resource supply, including copper, combined with a greater willingness by governments to procure commodities, tend to underpin pricing power.
